\section[\gu{મળીશું}]{\gu{મળીશું} (maḷīshũ) — \textquotedblleft{}(we) will meet\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C04-malishun}



\begin{quote}
A future-tense verb — the other half of \textquotedblleft{}see you again.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{મ}} (\emph{ma}) + \textbf{\gu{ળી}} (\emph{ḷī}, with the retroflex \textbf{\gu{ળ}} \emph{ḷ}) + \textbf{\gu{શું}} (\emph{shũ}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{મળીશું}} (\emph{maḷīshũ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{મળીશું}} (\emph{maḷīshũ}, \textquotedblleft{}we will meet\textquotedblright{}) is the future of \textbf{\gu{મળવું}} (\emph{maḷvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{}), from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{મિલ્}} (\emph{mil-}, \textquotedblleft{}to join, unite\textquotedblright{}) — the same root as Hindi \emph{milnā} and Punjabi \emph{milṇā}. Note the retroflex \textbf{\gu{ળ}} (\emph{ḷ}): Gujarati keeps this extra letter — like Marathi and the Dravidian south, and unlike Hindi. The ending \textbf{-\gu{શું}} (\emph{-shũ}) is the \textquotedblleft{}we will\textquotedblright{} future.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the future is an ending}]
Gujarati marks the future with an ending on the stem: \emph{maḷ-} (\textquotedblleft{}meet\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{-īshũ} (\textquotedblleft{}we will\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \emph{maḷīshũ}. No helper-word like English \textquotedblleft{}will.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}maḷīshũ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the verb it's from (\emph{maḷvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to meet,\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{mil-})
  \item the extra letter it shows (retroflex \gu{ળ}, \emph{ḷ})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb is \emph{maḷīshũ} from, and what special letter does it use? (\emph{Maḷvũ} \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{}; the retroflex \gu{ળ} \emph{ḷ}, which Hindi lacks.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{કાલે} \gu{મળીશું}]{\gu{કાલે} \gu{મળીશું} (kāle maḷīshũ) — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C04-kaale}



\begin{quote}
A goodbye for tomorrow — built on a word that means both \textbf{tomorrow} and \textbf{yesterday}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{કા}} (\emph{kā}) + \textbf{\gu{લે}} (\emph{le}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{કાલે}} (\emph{kāle}, \textquotedblleft{}on {[}the{]} \emph{kāl}\textquotedblright{}). The base is \textbf{\gu{કાલ}} (\emph{kāl}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{કાલ}} (\emph{kāl}) means \textbf{both \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{}} — the day on either side of today — from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{કાલ}} (\emph{kāla}, \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}). (It is the very same \emph{kāla} behind Hindi's \emph{kal}, Bengali's \emph{kāl}, and Punjabi's \emph{akāl} \textquotedblleft{}timeless.\textquotedblright{}) The verb's tense tells which: \emph{kāle maḷīshũ} (future $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tomorrow} we'll meet\textquotedblright{}), \emph{kāle maḷyā} (past $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}we met \textbf{yesterday}\textquotedblright{}). So \textbf{\gu{કાલે} \gu{મળીશું}} = \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow we'll meet\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kāle maḷīshũ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the puzzle — \emph{kāl} means both \textbf{tomorrow} and \textbf{yesterday}
  \item the root and its cousins (\emph{kāla} \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}; Hindi \emph{kal}, Punjabi \emph{akāl})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two opposite days does \emph{kāl} mean, and what tells them apart? (Both tomorrow and yesterday; the verb's tense.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{પાછા}]{\gu{પાછા} (pāchhā) — \textquotedblleft{}again, back\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C04-pachha}



\begin{quote}
One small word turns a goodbye into \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{till next time}.\textquotedblright{} You already have the other half — \emph{āvjo} (\textquotedblleft{}come again\textquotedblright{}) — from Chapter 1.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{પા}} (\emph{pā}) + \textbf{\gu{છા}} (\emph{chhā}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{પાછા}} (\emph{pāchhā}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{પાછા}} (\emph{pāchhā}, \textquotedblleft{}back, again, returning\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{પશ્ચાત્}} (\emph{paścāt}, \textquotedblleft{}behind, afterward\textquotedblright{}) — the same \textquotedblleft{}behind/after\textquotedblright{} root behind English \emph{post-} words, distantly. It carries the sense of \emph{return}: \emph{pāchhā āvvũ} (\textquotedblleft{}to come back\textquotedblright{}), \emph{pāchhā jāvũ} (\textquotedblleft{}to go back\textquotedblright{}). Add it to \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet\textquotedblright{} and you get the warm goodbye of the next lesson.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pāchhā\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it adds to a goodbye (\textquotedblleft{}again / back\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{pāchhā} mean, and what sense does it carry? (\textquotedblleft{}Back / again\textquotedblright{}; the sense of return — \emph{pāchhā āvvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to come back.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{પાછા} \gu{મળીશું}]{\gu{પાછા} \gu{મળીશું} (pāchhā maḷīshũ) — \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C04-pachha-malishun}



\begin{quote}
The warm, explicit goodbye — the companion of Chapter 1's \emph{āvjo}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{પાછા} \gu{મળીશું}} = \textbf{\gu{પાછા}} (\emph{pāchhā}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\gu{મળીશું}} (\emph{maḷīshũ}, \textquotedblleft{}we will meet\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{we'll meet again}.\textquotedblright{} Where Chapter 1's \textbf{\gu{આવજો}} (\emph{āvjo}) is the quick, warm \textquotedblleft{}come again,\textquotedblright{} \emph{pāchhā maḷīshũ} spells out the promise: we will meet once more. It is the same \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} the whole subcontinent prefers (Hindi \emph{phir milenge}, Bengali \emph{āshi}, Tamil \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the warm goodbye — \emph{pāchhā maḷīshũ}
  \item the two words it's built from (\emph{pāchhā} + \emph{maḷīshũ})
  \item the Chapter-1 goodbye it partners (\emph{āvjo})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{pāchhā maḷīshũ} literally say, and how does it relate to \emph{āvjo}? (\textquotedblleft{}We'll meet again\textquotedblright{}; it's the explicit form of Ch.1's \textquotedblleft{}come again\textquotedblright{} goodbye.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 4 — The farewells}

\label{lesson:GU-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three ways to part — none of them a blunt \textquotedblleft{}goodbye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the quick \textquotedblleft{}come again\textquotedblright{} (Chapter 1) — \emph{āvjo}
  \item the explicit \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} — \emph{pāchhā maḷīshũ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \emph{kāle maḷīshũ}
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\begin{cousinweb}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}(we) will meet\textquotedblright{} (\emph{pāchhā}, \emph{maḷīshũ})
  \item the word that means BOTH tomorrow and yesterday (\emph{kāl})
  \item the retroflex letter in \emph{maḷīshũ} (\gu{ળ}, \emph{ḷ})
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āvjo} (\textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}come {[}again{]},\textquotedblright{} from \emph{āvvũ} \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{maḷīshũ} $\leftarrow$ \emph{maḷvũ} \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{} (Sanskrit \emph{mil-}); the retroflex \gu{ળ}
  \item \emph{kāl} $\leftarrow$ \emph{kāla} \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} (Hindi \emph{kal}, Punjabi \emph{akāl})
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You're leaving a friend and will see them tomorrow. Give the goodbye and the \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} version. (\emph{Āvjo} — and \emph{kāle maḷīshũ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
